common_name: Opening Act Blush Garden Phlox (Compact Mounding Mildew-Resistant Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade with good air circulation; Opening Act was bred for a lower, more mounding habit and improved mildew resistance compared to older tall garden phlox.

directions: Opening Act Blush produces domed clusters of soft blush-pink flowers on a compact, well-branched plant that stays under 2 feet tall, considerably shorter than traditional garden phlox, which reduces the need for staking and fits smaller borders and containers. It was bred with improved resistance to the powdery mildew that disfigures many older phlox cultivars by midsummer, though good air circulation and consistent soil moisture still help keep foliage clean. Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade, and deadhead spent flower clusters to encourage continued bloom through summer. Its dense, mounding habit and fragrant flowers make it a strong front-of-border choice where taller phlox would overwhelm the space.

common_name: Li'l Bang Daybreak Coreopsis (Compact Red-Yellow Bicolor Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Li'l Bang Daybreak was bred for a compact, uniform habit and an extra-long bloom season compared to older coreopsis seed strains.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil in full sun; Li'l Bang Daybreak bears bright yellow daisy flowers marked with a red-maroon band at the base of each petal, giving a warm bicolor effect on a compact, tidy plant bred for uniformity and a long, heavy bloom season from late spring through fall. Deadheading spent flowers keeps the display fresh and encourages continued flowering, though the plant blooms prolifically even with minimal care. Like other coreopsis it is very drought-tolerant once established and performs best in lean, well-drained soil rather than rich or consistently wet ground. It is a strong nectar source for bees and small butterflies and works well massed in a sunny border or mixed into a pollinator planting.

common_name: Belleza Dark Pink Gaura (Compact Uniform Seed-Grown Gaura)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; Belleza Dark Pink was bred as a uniform, early-flowering seed strain of gaura for more predictable garden and container performance than older open-pollinated types.

directions: Belleza Dark Pink produces a cloud of small, four-petaled, deep rose-pink flowers on slender, wiry stems that dance in the slightest breeze, the same airy, naturalistic effect that has made Lindheimer's gaura a favorite Southern perennial, but bred from seed for a more compact, uniform habit and earlier flowering than older selections. Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; excellent drainage is essential, since gaura declines quickly in heavy or consistently wet soil. It blooms nearly continuously from spring through frost once established, drawing bees and small butterflies throughout the season, and its deep taproot makes it highly drought-tolerant. Cut back by about a third in midsummer if the plant becomes floppy or open, which encourages fresh, more compact regrowth and continued bloom.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Oenothera lindheimeri Native Plant
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Gaura lindheimeri for Texas Landscapes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil; Rosy Jane holds a more compact, well-branched form than the taller straight species.

directions: Rosy Jane bears rose-pink, four-petaled flowers that open from darker pink buds on wiry, arching stems, giving the same dancing, butterfly-like movement that gaura is known for but on a more compact, bushy plant than older tall selections. It flowers nearly continuously from spring through frost in zone 9 once established, drawing bees and small butterflies, and its deep taproot gives it excellent drought tolerance. Plant in full sun in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile soil, since good drainage matters far more to this plant's health than fertility, and wet or heavy soil quickly leads to root and crown rot. A midsummer trim of about a third of the plant's height keeps growth compact and encourages continued flowering into fall.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center — Oenothera lindheimeri Native Plant
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Gaura lindheimeri for Texas Landscapes
